Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Firefighter
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 68

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Emotional Stress: Situations that make me feel strong emotions, Redirection: I think of something else, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Threat: Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Vignette:
As she recounts her story, Captain Rachel Jenkins' eyes scan the room with a mixture of vigilance and unease. It's been two years since her life-threatening illness, a bout of sepsis that left her hospitalized for weeks, but the memories still feel like they're etched into her skin. The smell of hospitals, with its antiseptic tang, can transport her back to those endless days of beeping machines and sterile white sheets. Rachel's nose wrinkles in distaste as she recalls the overwhelming feeling of helplessness that gripped her during that time. Rachel's gaze drifts, and for a moment, it seems like she's staring right through the wall. "I remember lying there, unable to move or speak," she says, her voice barely above a whisper. "The needles and drips... they were everywhere. I felt like I was drowning in them." The image of medical equipment still haunts her; even a glimpse of a syringe on TV can send her heart racing. As a firefighter, Rachel's used to being in control, but the memories of her illness have left her feeling vulnerable. She avoids situations that might trigger strong emotions – it's easier to redirect her thoughts, focus on something else, than to risk feeling overwhelmed. Hospitals, ambulances, and medical examinations are now off-limits; she'll go out of her way to avoid them. Her colleagues at the fire station have noticed a change in her – Rachel used to be the first one to rush into a burning building, but lately, she's been more cautious, more hesitant. Rachel's constant scanning for danger has become second nature. She's always on high alert, her body tense and ready to react to any perceived threat. Her friends and family have commented on how jumpy she is – the way she'll flinch at a sudden noise or lunge out of bed in response to a creaking floorboard. Rachel knows it's not rational, but she can't shake off the feeling that something's lurking just around the corner. When memories of her illness surface, Rachel feels like she's right back in that hospital bed. Her body tenses up, and for an instant, she's paralyzed with fear. The terror she felt during those long days is still palpable – it's as if time has frozen, leaving her trapped in a never-ending nightmare. Putting the experience into words is almost impossible; Rachel can only shake her head, her eyes welling up with tears. It's been months since Rachel last went for a routine medical checkup. She knows she needs to get back on track, but the thought of sitting in an examination room, surrounded by the familiar smells and sounds of hospitals, makes her stomach twist into knots. Her husband has tried to reassure her, but Rachel can't shake off the feeling that she's just waiting for the other shoe to drop – that some new threat is lurking around the corner, just out of sight. As she looks back on the past two years, Rachel realizes that avoiding her fears hasn't made them disappear. If anything, they've grown stronger, more insidious. She knows it's time to confront them head-on, but the thought fills her with a sense of dread. What if she can't overcome this? What if she's stuck in this limbo forever? Rachel takes a deep breath and meets your gaze, her eyes searching for reassurance. "I just want to be able to go back to living my life," she says, her voice barely above a whisper. "I want to be able to walk into a hospital without feeling like I'm going to collapse. I want to be able to sleep through the night without waking up in a cold sweat." It's time for Rachel to face her fears and learn to navigate this new reality – with your help, she hopes to find a way out of this darkness and back into the light.
